paragraphs: §1 — The Jews' disagreement concerning Jesus

The Jews are much divided concerning "Jesus": some of them claim that he laid claim to prophethood, and some denied this. As for the Rabbanites — they reported in the Talmud that they conceded his miracles, but claimed the miracles were worked for him by "sorcery" and "the hidden Name." As for "Benjamin" [al-Nahāwandī], it was reported to me of him that he claims five men of the Jews laid claim to prophethood, one of them Jesus; he said: of them Scripture says [Dan 11:14]: "וּבְנֵי פָּרִיצֵי עַמְּךָ יִנַּשְּׂאוּ לְהַעֲמִיד חָזוֹן וְנִכְשָׁלוּ." As for some of the Karaites — they claim that "Jesus" was a righteous man, and that his case was like the case of "Zadok," "ʿAnan," and others; the Rabbanites set themselves to kill him until they killed him, just as they sought to kill "ʿAnan" too, only that they were not able. This is their way with everyone who wished to dissent from them. And Jesus forbade divorce, as the Sadducees forbade it.
§2 — Paul the founder

As for the religion of the Christians that they are upon now — "Paul" is the one who innovated it and brought it forth. He it is who ascribed divinity to "Jesus," and laid claim for himself to prophethood from "Jesus" his master. He brought no obligation at all and imposed nothing upon anyone, claiming that the religion is humility alone. They claim that fasting and prayer with them are not an obligation but voluntary; and he forbade nothing of foods, but permitted every animal — from the fly to the elephant.
§3 — The three hypostases

As for the religion of the Christians that they are upon now — it is standing irreligion. That is: they claim that the Creator is one substance with three hypostases (aqānīm), and that He is one [that is] three and three [that is] one. For He is, with them, living and knowing; so "living" and "knowing" are two attributes of an essence: the essence is one hypostasis, and the two attributes are two hypostases — so by this they become three hypostases.

They claim that the Messiah of whom the prophets gave glad tidings and whose coming was promised is "Jesus," and that he is one of the three hypostases. The three hypostases are: Son, Father, and Spirit. The Son is "Jesus," and he is divine-human; for the Creator — who is the essence — was united with him. This is the substance of their statements; they have differences in the details. They say that the House of which the prophets gave glad tidings that it would be built thereafter, and which "Ezekiel" beheld, is none other than what Zerubbabel built; and likewise all the glad tidings of which the prophets gave tidings have already passed and come to be.
§4 — The philosophers of the Christians

As for the "moderns" (the [latter-day] philosophers) of the Christians — they claim that the obligations of the Torah were imposed on the Children of Israel only by way of punishment, and that they themselves chose them because they resemble the obligations of the Ṣābians (the Ṣābiʾa); this was only because they had been constrained to the doctrines of the Egyptians when they grew up among them, which are of the kind of the doctrines of the Ṣābians. They claim that the statement that "the Creator — exalted — is one substance in three hypostases" is a secret that God did not disclose to anyone of the ancients, since the minds of men then could not contain it; until Jesus came, and men arose who could contain it in their minds, so He disclosed it to them and made it known to them. They claim that the Creator's speech is co-eternal with Him — one of the things they rely on in argument; for "John" says at the opening of his Gospel — one of the four Gospels [John 1:1]: "בְּרֵאשִׁית הָיָה הַדָּבָר וְהַדָּבָר הָיָה אֵצֶל הָאֱלֹהִים וֵאלֹהִים הָיָה הַדָּבָר." With this, they hang upon things from our books, which I shall mention later, after I have concluded against them and stated what is against them from the side of the intelligible.
§5 — David al-Muqammiṣ on the origin of the Christian religion

This is what "David son of Marwān al-Raqqī" reported of the origin of the religion of the Christians: "David son of Marwān al-Raqqī" — known as "al-Muqammiṣ" — was a philosopher; he was at first a Jew, and then converted to Christianity at Nisibis at the hands of a man called "Nānā." This "Nānā" was great among the Christians, for he was a complete philosopher whose craft was medicine. "David al-Muqammiṣ" studied with him for many years, mastered the principles and secrets of Christianity, and excelled in philosophy. He composed against the Christians two books in which he argued — both books well known. He also translated, from the books of the Christians and their commentaries, a commentary on Genesis, which he called "the Book of Creation," and a commentary on Ecclesiastes. "David son of Marwān" also said:

The Christians — when they did not find in the Gospel decisive rulings on some matter — claimed that "Paul" and "Peter," who is "Abū Shāwul," the Jewish fisherman, established for them limits and rulings not in the Gospel or in the Torah — except the Sabbath. These two men commanded their observance, and said that these rulings are rulings the Messiah handed to them, and decreed and ruled by them. And when these rulings that "Paul" and "Peter" established did not supply what was needed, bishops gathered in the city of "Nicaea," and established for them rulings the former had not transmitted; these became authoritative and accepted — though they have for them no text in the Torah, the Gospel, or the canon of "Peter" and "Paul." Yet with them they are God's rulings, by which they decide, though there is no decision in [Scripture]; he said: whoever examines this knows it. Nor were it only these three hundred and eighteen bishops who established this for them; others established [rulings] for them too. He said: the cause of this is that their Gospel constrained them to believe the statement of every possessor of an opinion, with no argument from the Gospel.

§7 — The Gospels and their contradictions
[Jesus said, Matt 5:17]: "I have not come to abolish [the Torah and the Prophets] but to fulfill. And whoever annuls one commandment of them shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven."

As for the four Gospels: they are the Gospel of "Matthew," of "Mark," of "Luke," and of "John." As for "Matthew," he was a man of the toll-house (a tax-collector); "Mark" was a fisherman who caught fish from the lake of Tiberias; "Luke" was a disciple of "Paul" — who is "Abū Shāwul" — and was a physician; and "Paul" was a leather-worker. As for "John," he came after Jesus, and was of the kin of the one who had charge of Jesus in what he had charge of. He [al-Muqammiṣ] said: this Gospel is a book in which these [four] relate the story of "Jesus" from its beginning to its end: his coming, from whom he was born, and his genealogy. These four Gospels agree in [some] things and disagree in [others]. They disagree in the genealogy: for "Matthew" reckoned forefathers other than the forefathers "Luke" reckoned, while "Mark" mentioned no forefathers and no genealogy, and likewise "John." [Matthew traced the ascent upward — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron — down to David; Luke, [tracing] a natural genealogy down to David, then departs from the line "Matthew" reckoned by passing from "Solomon" to "Nathan" son of David; and the genealogy each gives is the genealogy of Joseph, the betrothed of "the mother of Jesus."]

So there are here three difficulties: the first — two differing genealogies of Jesus; the second — that both are genealogies of Joseph, not of Jesus; the third — that if "the mother of Jesus" had no husband Joseph, then their genealogies do not fit: for they claim that Mary the mother of Jesus "was betrothed" to Joseph and that Joseph did not come in to her, but found her pregnant — so the statement of "Matthew" and "Luke" [makes the conception] "from the Holy Spirit."

No mention of "Heli," "Jacob," and "Matthat" is found in the twenty-four books, nor in the historians of the Jews — neither in general nor [as] known in any genealogy. So the Christians contrived, and said that "Heli" is a man of theirs, "son of Nathan" born of David, and was the brother of "Jacob son of Nathan" born of "Solomon," his maternal brother; that the man "Heli" died childless, so "Jacob" his maternal brother came in to his wife and raised up seed for him — and "Joseph" was born. So Joseph was the son of the two men: of "Jacob" by nature, and of "Heli" by the imputation that is the raising up of seed. This is the statement of "David son of Marwān al-Muqammiṣ," which I have reported as it is, to show by it the unsoundness and weakness of the Christians' case. With this — the matter is too plain and clear to need elaboration.

: Arabic Faulus, the Apostle Paul. Q takes the (anti-Jewish) view that Paul is the founder of Christianity — a position developed later in medieval Jewish anti-Christian polemic.
: An allusion to the abrogation of the dietary obligations in Christianity, as against Judaism.

: The doctrine of the Trinity. Q deploys the Muslim/kalām polemic: if God is "living" and "knowing," these are attributes of a single divine essence and do not become separate persons. Cf. Saadia, Beliefs and Opinions, and Lasker, "Karaism and the Jewish-Christian Debate" (2012).
: The Ṣābiʾa (Ṣābians), a pre-Islamic Mesopotamian sect of star-worshippers; Q treats them further in Maqala IV. Cf. EI³, "Ṣābiʾa."
: The opening of the Gospel of John ("In the beginning was the Word"), which Q cites as one of the Christians' theological supports — that the Word (logos) is co-eternal in God.
: David b. Marwān al-Muqammiṣ (10th c.), author of the "Book of Creation" (a commentary on Genesis) and two anti-Christian polemics. See Stroumsa, Dāwūd b. Marwān al-Muqammiṣ's Twenty Chapters.
: Nisibis, a city of northern Mesopotamia and an early Christian center.
: The Council of Nicaea (325 CE). Q gives the traditional figure of 318 bishops — a number that is also the gematria of "אֱלִיעֶזֶר" (cf. Gen 14:14).
: Arabic sarrāj, a leather-/saddle-worker.
